verses.1: A psalm of David. The earth is the LORD'S and all it holds, the world and those who live there.
verses.2: For God founded it on the seas, established it over the rivers.
verses.3: Who may go up the mountain of the LORD? Who can stand in his holy place?
verses.4: "The clean of hand and pure of heart, who are not devoted to idols, who have not sworn falsely.
verses.5: They will receive blessings from the LORD, and justice from their saving God.
verses.6: Such are the people that love the LORD, that seek the face of the God of Jacob." Selah
verses.7: Lift up your heads, O gates; rise up, you ancient portals, that the king of glory may enter.
verses.8: Who is this king of glory? The LORD, a mighty warrior, the LORD, mighty in battle.
verses.9: Lift up your heads, O gates; rise up, you ancient portals, that the king of glory may enter.
verses.10: Who is this king of glory? The LORD of hosts is the king of glory. Selah

notes.text: Literally, "the one whose hands are clean." The singular is used for the entire class of worshipers, hence the plural translation.

Lift up your heads, O gates... you ancient portals: the literal meaning is impossible since the portcullis (a gate that moves up and down) was unknown in the ancient world. Extra-biblical parallels suggest a full personification of the circle of gate towers: they are like a council of elders, bowed down and anxious, awaiting the return of the army and the Great Warrior gone to battle.
